derived.prompt: Does TCP use a handshake to set up a connection between the two hosts?
bridge: A connectionless protocol neither sets up nor closes a connection: it sends each packet on its own.
derived.determinacy_why: No in every world: the edit puts TCP among connectionless protocols, and the class rule gives its members no connection setup. TCP's three-way handshake is a side fact of TCP that goes with the edit; a model that keeps it holds TCP as a connectionless protocol that sets up connections, the inconsistent patch, not a world.

chain: A connectionless protocol neither sets up nor closes a connection: it sends each packet on its own. (stored, class rule)
So there is no TCP connection to close: no.

TCP is a connection-oriented protocol..why: Stated in the lead of the TCP article and in every networking textbook; usually set against UDP, "a connectionless protocol". It follows from nothing a model would hold apart from TCP's own handshake, which is part of the same description.

sources.quote: TCP is connection-oriented, meaning that sender and receiver first need to establish a connection based on agreed parameters; they do this through a three-way handshake procedure.

HTTP/1.1 runs over TCP..why: HTTP before HTTP/3 runs over TCP; stated in the HTTP article and in RFC 9112.

sources.quote: The standard choice of the underlying protocol prior to HTTP/3 is Transmission Control Protocol (TCP).

notes: Stored edit (very_unlikely): TCP being connection-oriented is stated everywhere, usually set against UDP. Chosen for ABox inheritance: the edit moves an individual (TCP) from one class to another, and both determinate queries ask what the new class gives its members (no connection setup, no connection to close). The class rule is definitional for "connectionless" and has no exceptions. TCP's handshake and teardown are side facts of TCP itself and go with the edit; keeping them is the inconsistent patch, not a world. The background split is HTTP/1.1's transport, stored by name (stays on TCP) or as "a connection-oriented transport" (leaves TCP). The prompts say HTTP/1.1, since HTTP/3 runs over QUIC. The setup query asks about the handshake, not about data waiting for it, since TCP Fast Open lets data ride in the SYN. Near query (TCP's layer) is not affected by the mode and its answer differs from the new answer. R2: no prompt names the mode except the direct and paraphrase questions, which offer both. 'Runs over' is many-valued in general; the HTTP/1.1 questions ('the transport protocol HTTP/1.1 normally runs over') presuppose one transport, which is a stated bridge with a check (2026-10-31, formal check FINDINGS C3).
